title: A neighbourhood quiet-hour agreement
paragraphs: Residents of Maple Court had complained for months about late-night noise from deliveries, parties and people using the shared courtyard. The building manager first proposed a strict rule banning all courtyard use after nine in the evening, but several residents argued that this would punish people who used the space quietly after work.

A resident committee instead collected examples of the main problems. They found that most complaints involved amplified music, group events and delivery vehicles waiting with engines running. Ordinary conversation was rarely mentioned. The committee therefore proposed a quieter-hours agreement focused on specific behaviour rather than simply closing the space.

The agreement asks residents to avoid amplified sound after ten, register large gatherings in advance and ask delivery drivers not to leave engines running. It also creates a contact system so residents can report a problem to the building before calling outside authorities. Critics say the rules rely too much on cooperation, while supporters argue that flexible rules are more likely to be accepted and followed.

After three months, formal complaints have fallen, although the committee warns that one successful season does not prove the policy will always work. They plan to review the agreement during summer, when more people use the courtyard late in the evening. The aim, they say, is not silence but a shared standard that allows different routines to coexist.

questions.prompt: Why was the manager's first proposal criticized?
options: It allowed loud music all night.
It would ban all late courtyard use, including quiet use.
It required more delivery vehicles.
It closed the building during the day.
questions.explanationJa: problem behaviourだけでなくquiet useまで一律禁止するためです。

questions.prompt: Give two main sources of complaints identified by the committee.
markscheme: Amplified music and/or large group events.
Delivery vehicles waiting with engines running.

questions.prompt: True or false: Ordinary conversation was a major source of complaints.
questions.justification: The committee found that ordinary conversation was rarely mentioned in complaints.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。ordinary conversationはrarely mentionedでした。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 4 meaning 'to exist together at the same time or place'.
In paragraph 3, what does 'the rules' refer to?
options: The quieter-hours agreement and its behaviour-based requirements
National traffic law
School rules
Rental prices

questions.prompt: How does the new agreement differ from the original ban? Give two ideas.
markscheme: It targets specific noisy behaviours instead of banning all courtyard use after a fixed time.
It relies on advance registration, cooperation and an internal contact system rather than only prohibition.
questions.explanationJa: blanket banからbehaviour-specific rulesへ変わりました。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: The aim is not silence but a shared ________.
What is the committee's attitude toward the early results?
options: It sees them as final proof of success.
It is encouraged but remains cautious and plans further review.
It considers the policy a failure.
It wants to remove all rules immediately.
questions.explanationJa: complaints減少を評価しつつseasonal reviewが必要としています。

questions.prompt: What broader idea about community rules does the report present? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Rules can be more effective when they target the actual source of conflict rather than applying broad restrictions to everyone.
Community cooperation and review can help balance different routines, although flexibility may depend on compliance.

title: Students decide part of the budget
paragraphs: A high school has given students control over ten thousand dollars of its annual improvement budget. Students cannot use the money for salaries or compulsory safety work, but they can propose projects related to learning spaces, recreation or student wellbeing.

In the first year, proposals included more outdoor seating, a podcast studio and free hygiene products in bathrooms. Student teams had to explain cost, expected users and maintenance. The most popular idea in an online vote was the podcast studio, but the student budget committee discovered that soundproofing would use almost the entire fund.

Instead of automatically funding the winning idea, the committee asked the team to redesign it. The revised proposal used a smaller recording room and shared equipment already owned by the music department. This left enough money for hygiene products and shaded outdoor tables as well.

Some students complained that changing the winning proposal weakened democracy. The principal responded that participation means making decisions within real constraints, not simply choosing from a wish list. The school will repeat the project next year and publish both the voting results and the final spending decisions so students can see how preferences, costs and feasibility interact.

questions.prompt: What limitation is placed on the student-controlled budget?
options: Students may spend it only on salaries.
It cannot be used for salaries or compulsory safety work.
Only teachers may propose ideas.
No maintenance information is required.
questions.explanationJa: salaryやmandatory safety workには使えません。

questions.prompt: What information did proposal teams have to provide? Give two examples.
True or false: The most popular proposal was funded exactly as first submitted.
questions.justification: The podcast-studio proposal was redesigned because soundproofing would have consumed almost the entire budget.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。cost constraintに合わせてredesignされました。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 4 meaning 'practical possibility of being successfully carried out'.
In paragraph 3, what does 'This' refer to?
options: Using a smaller recording room and shared existing equipment
Cancelling the budget
Increasing the fund
Removing outdoor seating

questions.prompt: Why did the committee redesign the podcast proposal? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: The original soundproofing cost would have used almost all available money.
Reducing the studio cost allowed the budget to support additional projects for more students.
questions.explanationJa: resource constraintとopportunity costの問題です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Participation means making decisions within real ________.
What is the principal's view of democratic participation?
options: The most popular idea must always be funded unchanged.
Participation includes balancing preferences with costs and feasibility.
Students should never see final spending decisions.
Voting is the only useful part of participation.
questions.explanationJa: preferenceだけでなくcost/feasibilityもdecisionの一部としています。

questions.prompt: Why will the school publish both votes and spending decisions? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Students can see whether popular preferences influenced the outcome.
They can also see how costs and practical constraints changed or limited the final decision.

title: A library without money fines
paragraphs: The city library of Norfield has stopped charging daily late fees for most books. Borrowers are still expected to return items on time, and accounts are temporarily blocked if a book is more than three weeks overdue. The change is intended to remove small debts that sometimes kept families from returning to the library at all.

Before the policy changed, staff found that many people with overdue fines were not heavy users trying to exploit the system. Some had simply forgotten a book, moved house or struggled to pay several small charges that had accumulated. Children could also lose access because a parent was unable or unwilling to clear a family account.

Critics predicted that returns would become slower once the financial penalty disappeared. During the first six months, average return time changed very little. Staff believe the temporary borrowing block still provides a strong reason to return books. However, the library has not eliminated responsibility: people who lose an item must still replace it or agree on another solution.

The library is now examining a different question: whether removing fines changes who uses the service. Early data shows an increase in returning borrowers from lower-income neighbourhoods, but staff say longer-term evidence is needed. They want to know not only whether books come back, but whether the rules support access without reducing the shared responsibility that allows a public collection to function.

questions.prompt: What happens when a book is more than three weeks overdue?
options: The borrower is permanently banned.
The account is temporarily blocked from further borrowing.
The book becomes the borrower's property.
A daily fine doubles.
questions.explanationJa: daily fineではなくtemporary borrowing blockです。

questions.prompt: Give two reasons small fines could reduce access to the library.
markscheme: Small charges could accumulate into a debt that some families struggled to pay.
Children or family members could lose access because another person could not clear the account.

questions.prompt: True or false: Removing daily fines caused a large increase in average return time.
questions.justification: During the first six months, average return time changed very little.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。return timeはほぼ変化していません。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 2 meaning 'built up gradually over time'.
In paragraph 3, what does 'the financial penalty' refer to?
options: Daily late fees
The temporary borrowing block
The cost of library membership
The price of replacing every book

questions.prompt: How does the new system still encourage responsibility? Give two details.
markscheme: Accounts can be blocked when books are seriously overdue, creating an incentive to return them.
Lost items still have to be replaced or resolved through another agreed solution.
questions.explanationJa: fineをなくしてもaccount blockとlost-item responsibilityは残ります。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Staff want to know whether the rules support ________ without reducing shared responsibility.
Why are staff cautious about the increase in returning borrowers?
options: The data is impossible to collect.
They need longer-term evidence before concluding the policy caused a lasting access change.
Lower-income users are not allowed to borrow books.
Return times doubled.
questions.explanationJa: early dataだけでcausationを断定していません。

questions.prompt: What balance is the library trying to achieve? Give two sides.
markscheme: Reduce financial barriers so more people can access and return to the library.
Maintain shared responsibility so books are returned or replaced and the public collection continues to function.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main purpose?
options: To argue that borrowed books need no rules
To examine whether a no-daily-fine policy can improve access while preserving responsibility
To advertise private bookstores
To prove fines are the only reason books are returned
questions.explanationJa: fine-free policyのtrade-offを検討するfeatureです。
